paragraphs.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.

paragraphs.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

items.text: Start with the one-year trial you propose in paragraph 5. Bring that proposal into paragraph 1 where you currently announce the debate. Which reason from your commute or your roommate’s experience makes the trial worth doing? Give that reason in your own words. Return to the trial in the conclusion and explain how the council should judge it.

Check the source behind the Riverton example in paragraph 2. Record who reported the ridership change, by how much it changed, and over what period. Check whether the source also identifies which riders returned. Use only what you can verify, then explain what Riverton helps you predict about the 14 and 22. If you can’t verify the example, build on the $64 up-front cost and your roommate’s walk.

Answer the cost objection in paragraph 3. Check what the one-fifth figure covers. What would the city need to replace for these two routes for one year? Look in the budget or council materials for a funding option you can support. Explain the trade-off and acknowledge any cost you can’t pin down.

Read paragraph 4 alongside your observation that the 22 fills up before the hospital. What would have to happen for free fares to reduce the number of cars at Grant Street? Connect that reasoning to your trial and check what the council report actually supports. Either develop the crowding point and connect extra service to cost, or cut the last sentence.

Check your meeting notes for the remark about keeping riders “respectful.” If you keep it, identify who made the point, clarify what they meant, and decide how your observation on the 22 answers it. If you can’t trace it, use that space for the funding objection.

Review the three grammar suggestions after revising. In paragraphs 2 and 3, read each side of the flagged comma on its own. If both sides can stand as sentences, they need a stronger join. In paragraph 4, check the verb against the plural subject “riders.”

Before submitting, check the length. The peer-review draft is 391 words and the final target is about 1,000. Use the added space to interpret your evidence and work through the funding objection. Reread the opening and ending together, then submit your version by 11:59 p.m.

paragraphs.text: Last month the city council debated whether to make the 14 and 22 bus lines free for riders. Supporters packed the meeting, and so did a few business owners who were worried about the cost. This essay will look at both sides of the free-bus debate. I take the 22 to campus every morning, so I have seen who rides it and who does not. Most mornings the bus is full before it reaches the hospital stop.

paragraphs.text: Fares are a bigger barrier than most people think, a monthly pass costs $64, which is more than many students spend on food in a week. A pass is cheaper per ride than single fares, but only if you can pay $64 at once. My roommate walks forty minutes to her job to save the fare, and some weeks she cannot afford the pass at all. When Riverton made its buses free two years ago, ridership went up. People who had stopped riding came back, especially older residents and part-time workers. Free fares would also save drivers the time they spend making change.

paragraphs.text: The main objection is cost. Fares pay for about a fifth of the system, and the city would have to replace that money from somewhere. This is a fair point, and I understand why people worry about it. Some council members said a small fee keeps riders respectful, I do not think that is true. Most of the people I see on the 22 are tired, not rude.

paragraphs.text: Free buses would also help the environment. More riders means fewer cars downtown and less traffic near the hospital, where ambulances get stuck every afternoon. On my route I count at least ten cars for every bus at the Grant Street light. The council's own report says the downtown streets are already over capacity at rush hour. Cleaner air matters to everyone who lives near Grant Street. Buses would get crowded, but the city could add more.

items.text: Start with the one-year trial you propose in paragraph 5. Bring that proposal into paragraph 1 where you currently announce the debate. Which reason from your commute or your roommate’s experience makes the trial worth doing? Give that reason in your own words. Return to the trial in the conclusion and explain how the council should judge it.

Check the source behind the Riverton example in paragraph 2. Record who reported the ridership change, by how much it changed, and over what period. Check whether the source also identifies which riders returned. Use only what you can verify, then explain what Riverton helps you predict about the 14 and 22. If you can’t verify the example, build on the $64 up-front cost and your roommate’s walk.

Answer the cost objection in paragraph 3. Check what the one-fifth figure covers. What would the city need to replace for these two routes for one year? Look in the budget or council materials for a funding option you can support. Explain the trade-off and acknowledge any cost you can’t pin down.

Read paragraph 4 alongside your observation that the 22 fills up before the hospital. What would have to happen for free fares to reduce the number of cars at Grant Street? Connect that reasoning to your trial and check what the council report actually supports. Either develop the crowding point and connect extra service to cost, or cut the last sentence.

Check your meeting notes for the remark about keeping riders “respectful.” If you keep it, identify who made the point, clarify what they meant, and decide how your observation on the 22 answers it. If you can’t trace it, use that space for the funding objection.

Review the three grammar suggestions after revising. In paragraphs 2 and 3, read each side of the flagged comma on its own. If both sides can stand as sentences, they need a stronger join. In paragraph 4, check the verb against the plural subject “riders.”

Before submitting, check the length. The peer-review draft is 391 words and the final target is about 1,000. Use the added space to interpret your evidence and work through the funding objection. Reread the opening and ending together, then submit your version by 11:59 p.m.

If you can’t verify the Riverton figure, your roommate’s forty-minute walk gives you a concrete example of what the fare costs a rider.
